paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder of neonatal diabetes and small bowel atresia, often associated with intestinal malabsorption (summary by Piccand et al., 2014). Other features include hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and jejunal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia (Mitchell et al., 2004). Several patients have had clusters of chromogranin A-positive, hormone-negative cells in the pancreas (summary by Piccand et al., 2014). Diabetes may also begin in childhood rather than in the neonatal period (Sansbury et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants from 3 families (2 sib pairs and an isolated case) with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia. The parents of one sib pair were consanguineous. Four children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. One patient had a milder form and was surviving without insulin. Pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 of the infants showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but complete absence of insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin. Exocrine histology was variable.

paragraphs.text: Concepcion et al. (2014) described a male infant born at 34 weeks' gestation to nonconsanguineous Vietnamese parents. Prenatally he had intrauterine growth restriction and duodenal atresia. He was small for gestational age (birth weight 1375 g) and had severe hyperglycemia (446 mg/dL) within 24 hours of birth, which needed an insulin infusion. He had low C-peptide, low amylase and lipase, and low stool pancreatic elastase. Laparotomy on day 5 confirmed duodenal atresia, intestinal malrotation, and jejunal perforation, and ultrasound suggested an annular pancreas. His course included cholestatic jaundice, recurrent infections, feeding intolerance, and severe chronic diarrhea that needed intermittent parenteral nutrition and did not improve with pancreatic enzymes. Laparotomy at 3 months showed gallbladder agenesis. A hepatobiliary scan did not visualize the gallbladder or common bile duct, and liver biopsy showed bile ductular proliferation. He developed liver failure and died of sepsis at 5 months of age while awaiting liver transplantation.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome whose diabetes was diagnosed at ages 3 and 6 years rather than in the neonatal period. The first, a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation, had duodenal atresia, jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. She had hyperglycemia at age 2 and presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at age 3, with very low insulin and C-peptide and negative autoantibodies. She also had an absent gallbladder and gastrointestinal bleeding due to gastric heterotopia in the small bowel. Her cousin, a boy born at 34 weeks with duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation, had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia at age 5 and was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6. He also had chronic iron deficiency anemia. Neither child had liver disease, and both were alive at age 9 years.

paragraphs.text: Zegre Amorim et al. (2015) reported a girl born to first-cousin Gipsy parents. Prenatal ultrasound showed intrauterine growth restriction and a 'double bubble.' She was born at 35 weeks with weight, length, and head circumference below the 3rd centile. She developed hyperglycemia on day 2 and needed continuous insulin. On day 3, insulin and C-peptide levels were very low, and GAD, islet cell, and IA-2 autoantibodies were negative. Laparotomy on day 4 confirmed type II duodenal atresia with annular pancreas, malrotation, and gallbladder agenesis. Cholestasis began on day 6, with conjugated bilirubin of 3.07 mg/dL and GGT of 458 IU/L, and resolved without treatment by 2 months of age. Ultrasound showed biliary duct dilation, and the head of the pancreas was disproportionately large with an unidentifiable tail. At surgery, perijejunal submucosal tissue that looked like ectopic pancreatic tissue was seen. The authors described this as a novel feature, but the tissue was not biopsied. The patient had chronic diarrhea and malabsorption that did not respond to exocrine pancreatic supplementation. At 7 months she had failure to thrive and still depended on insulin and partial parenteral nutrition.

paragraphs.text: In proband 2 (see Mapping), the child of consanguineous parents, Smith et al. (2010) used array capture and deep sequencing of the exons within the 3 shared HBD regions. Of 30 novel variants, the only nonsynonymous change was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in RFX6, which direct sequencing confirmed. Smith et al. (2010) then sequenced the 19 exons and splice junctions of RFX6 directly and found missense, splicing, or frameshift mutations in 5 of 6 available probands with the syndrome. Proband 1, the child of first cousins, was homozygous for a splice donor mutation in intron 2 (IVS2+2T-C). Proband 3 was compound heterozygous for 2 splice mutations (IVS6+2T-G and IVS1-12A-G). Proband 4 was homozygous for an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7, and proband 5 was homozygous for an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) missense mutation. All mutations were inherited from carrier parents. In EMSA, the R181Q mutation completely abolished DNA binding by RFX6, whereas S217P only modestly reduced DNA binding.

In contrast, the authors' patient, who was homozygous for K260T, had disease as severe as that of patients with homozygous splice site, frameshift, or DNA-binding-abolishing mutations. They noted that chronic diarrhea had been reported in most patients with RFX6 mutations.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) found that Rfx6 is expressed broadly in the definitive endoderm and later becomes restricted to the gut and pancreatic bud. It acts downstream of neurogenin-3 (Neurog3) and upstream of many islet transcription factors, and is required for the differentiation of 4 of the 5 islet cell types. Mutations in both RFX6 and NEUROG3 cause diarrhea and diabetes. The authors attributed the small bowel atresia and biliary abnormalities, which are seen only with RFX6 mutation, to Rfx6 expression in the early gut endoderm, where neurogenin-3 is not expressed.

paragraphs.text: Chandra et al. (2014) showed that RFX6 is present in adult human pancreatic endocrine cells. In the human beta-cell line EndoC-betaH2, RFX6 regulated insulin gene transcription, insulin content, and insulin secretion. Knocking down RFX6 lowered expression of calcium-channel genes and reduced L-type calcium-channel activity, which suppressed depolarization-evoked insulin exocytosis.

paragraphs.text: Piccand et al. (2014) showed that islets of mice with Rfx6 deleted in adult beta cells (Rfx6-deltaBeta mice) had strongly reduced Gck (glucokinase) and Abcc8/SUR1 transcripts, together with reduced Ucn3, NeuroD1, and Pax6. Slc2a2/Glut2, Pcsk1, and Kcnj11/Kir6.2 were unaltered. ChIP-seq and quantitative ChIP in Min6B1 beta cells showed that endogenous Rfx6 binds X-boxes in the Gck promoter and in intron 10 of Abcc8, suggesting that Rfx6 directly and positively regulates transcription of these genes. Multicellular imaging of intact islets showed that glucose-induced intracellular calcium responses were reduced by 50 to 60% and glucose-induced cytosolic ATP/ADP increases by about 60% in Rfx6-deleted beta cells. RNA sequencing showed downregulation of 8 voltage-dependent calcium channel transcripts (including Cacna1a, Cacnb2, Cacna1d, and Cacna1c), and ChIP studies showed Rfx6 binding to X-boxes in intron 1 of Cacna1c and Cacnb2. In addition, 54 of the 68 known 'disallowed' genes, which are normally selectively repressed in mature mouse beta cells, were upregulated in Rfx6-deltaBeta islets, including Slc16a1, Ldha, Pdgfra, and Igfbp4. Rfx6 bound a conserved region about 10 kb upstream of Ldha. The authors proposed that Rfx6 acts as a master repressor that helps maintain beta cell maturity and functional identity.

(2014) suggested that patients with neonatal diabetes carrying RFX6 mutations are likely to have functional defects in their remaining beta cells, in addition to having fewer beta cells. They suggested that it might be worth investigating whether such individuals respond to pharmacologic treatments, including sulfonylureas or GLP-1 analogs, that could prompt insulin release from the remaining beta cells.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice by replacing the first 5 exons, which include the DNA-binding domain, with an eGFP-cre cassette. Homozygous mice were born at the expected mendelian ratio but fed poorly, had gross bowel distension from small bowel obstruction, and died within 2 days of birth. Some had a reduced pancreas size. At embryonic day 17.5, mutant pancreata contained many chromogranin A-positive endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin. Pancreatic polypeptide-expressing cells were increased.

paragraphs.text: Piccand et al. (2014) generated a floxed Rfx6 allele and deleted it in endocrine progenitors with Ngn3-Cre (Rfx6-deltaEndo mice). Like the full-body knockout, mutant pups were diabetic and died between 2 and 3 days after birth. Insulin-, glucagon-, somatostatin-, and ghrelin-expressing cells were nearly absent, PP cells were spared, and chromogranin A-positive, hormone-negative cells were present in the pancreas. The authors concluded that Rfx6 function downstream of Ngn3 is essential for beta cell generation and that impaired beta cell development does not result from defective endoderm.

paragraphs.text: Piccand et al. (2014) also inactivated Rfx6 in the adult beta cells of 8- to 10-week-old mice (Rfx6fl/fl; Ins1-CreERT2, Rfx6-deltaBeta) by tamoxifen treatment, achieving 95% deletion within 5 days. The mutant mice did not develop overt diabetes, and insulin, C-peptide 1, and C-peptide 2 remained detectable. Ins1 transcripts were reduced by approximately 54 to 65%, while Ins2 was unchanged. Rfx6-deltaBeta mice had normal fasting and fed blood glucose but significant glucose intolerance on both intraperitoneal and oral glucose tolerance testing. First- and second-phase glucose-induced insulin secretion was markedly reduced in vivo, and glucose- and KCl-stimulated insulin secretion was reduced in isolated islets. Beta cell mass, alpha cell mass, and beta cell proliferation were unaffected. The authors concluded that induced inactivation of Rfx6 in a mature beta cell does not preclude insulin production.

paragraphs.text: Martinez-Frias et al. (1992) described 2 Spanish sibs born to consanguineous parents with a multiple congenital anomaly pattern that included low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. They suggested that the constellation represented a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. A computerized search of the Spanish Collaborative Study of Congenital Malformations (ECEMC) found 3 other unrelated infants with intestinal atresias, hypospadias, and low birth weight. The authors suggested that these infants might represent a milder expression of the same syndrome. Smith et al. (2010) considered Martinez-Frias syndrome distinct from Mitchell-Riley syndrome (see Nomenclature).

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) studied proband 2, the child of consanguineous parents. Using array capture and deep sequencing of the exons within 3 shared homozygous regions, they found a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in the RFX6 gene. It was the only nonsynonymous change among 30 novel variants, and direct sequencing confirmed it. The variant lies between the DNA-binding and dimerization domains. In EMSA it only modestly reduced DNA binding, and it did not affect dimer formation. The patient was alive at age 4.5 years.

paragraphs.text: In a Vietnamese boy with Mitchell-Riley syndrome, Concepcion et al. (2014) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous c.779A-C transversion in the RFX6 gene, resulting in a lys260-to-thr (K260T) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation, and both parents were heterozygous carriers. The variant was absent from the dbSNP and 1000 Genomes databases. It affects a highly conserved lysine and was predicted to be damaging. It also changes the consensus 5-prime splice donor site of intron 7 and was predicted to disrupt splicing. The patient died at 5 months of age.

paragraphs.text: In 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes, Sansbury et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygosity for 2 nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene. One was a c.2176C-T transition in exon 17, resulting in an arg726-to-ter (R726X) substitution. The other was R866X. The mutations were found by targeted next-generation sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The authors predicted that the R726X mutation would be subject to nonsense-mediated decay. The fathers were heterozygous for R726X, and the mutation was traced back to a grandmother.

paragraphs.text: In 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes, Sansbury et al. (2015) found compound heterozygosity for the R726X mutation and a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18 of the RFX6 gene, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution. The R866X mutation was inherited from the mothers. Because it lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary, the authors predicted that it escapes nonsense-mediated decay and yields a partially truncated protein that keeps the entire DNA-binding domain and may retain some function. They suggested that this residual function might explain the later onset of diabetes and the otherwise milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with Mitchell-Riley syndrome born to consanguineous Gipsy parents, Zegre Amorim et al. (2015) used Sanger sequencing to identify a homozygous c.541C-T transition in exon 4 of the RFX6 gene, resulting in an arg181-to-trp (R181W) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The arginine at codon 181 lies in the DNA-binding domain and is highly conserved across species. The authors noted that a different mutation at the same residue (R181Q) had been reported previously.
